title: When Market Narratives Flip Overnight - Systematic Investor - Ep.390

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/When Market Narratives Flip Overnight - Systematic Investor - Ep.390.docx

summary: Top Traders Unplugged Ep.390 (Mar 2026): bonds and narratives flip from AI disinflation to Iran-driven stagflation; trend vs 60/40 sources of diversification and crisis attribution; 2025 lessons (narrative, resulting, staying with trends); AI-productivity analogy with Greenspan and the Warsh Fed; Winton papers on tracking error and CTA portfolio construction.

coverage.note: intro; bonds flip from disinflation to stagflation, Iran
Iran market reaction, option pinning, dispersion, Denmark politics
AlphaQuest closing, pod shops, short-term CTAs
pod shop capital, Jerry Parker on position sizing, listener question on crisis alpha
trend vs 60/40, two sources of diversification, crisis examples
low correlation to 60/40, crisis sector attribution, trend barometer, sectors
trend performance dispersion, hedge fund conference observations
return stacking, TPA, narrative change, CTA sentiment, record eight positive months
AI/Anthropic anecdote, TPA, energy positioning flip
performance numbers, March leaders, Citrini report, Warsh view
Greenspan 1990s productivity analogy, AI supply and demand effects
AI and Fed policy framework, labor mismatch, policy-error risk
Warsh appointment politics, Fed pressure, 2025 lessons begin
narrative vs statistics, drawdown timing, diversification not insurance, resulting
staying with trends, midfielder analogy, intro to Winton papers
Winton paper on tracking error and building a CTA portfolio
non-trend signals, one vs many managers, replication vs convexity
smooth ride, relationship cost, CTA beta question, outro

completeness_estimate: 0.87 - the first reader caught nearly every main thread (trend vs 60/40, narrative flips, AI-Fed analogy, Winton papers, performance data); missed several caveats and time-bound details and overstated one causal link.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: we did see bond markets move up last week on that kind of disinflationary theme
claims.claim: The Citrini report on AI-driven white-collar job losses pushed bonds up on a disinflation theme, then within a week Middle East/Iran fear reversed it, showing how fast narratives flip.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: equities have been down and bonds have been down at the same time as that kind of stagflationary fear has come back into the market
claims.claim: Stagflation fear from the oil shock made equities and bonds fall together, removing the usual bond hedge; 10y yields rebounded from below 4%.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: Iran is actually pretty muted. The way we've seen the big reaction has really been in the commodities and of course energy in particular
claims.claim: Financial markets reacted little to Iran events; the big move was in commodities and energy, with possible surprises ahead.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: the kind of pinning in the US equity indices and how option flows are keeping the market in a range
claims.claim: Option flows pin US equity indices in a range, so price action must be read alongside option expiry and flows, not just macro.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: seemingly low vol on the surface actually means probably more dispersion and more vol in the underlying securities
claims.claim: Low index vol implies higher dispersion and vol underneath in single stocks.
claims.indicator: index vol vs implied correlation / dispersion

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: I just wonder if if the pot shops and the rise of pot shops and the way they trade and the way they I wouldn't say manipulate the market but they certainly affect the markets
claims.claim: Niels speculates that multi-manager pod shops affect market behavior in a way that hurts some CTAs, as AlphaQuest (25+ years) returned capital.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: it's not a drawdown they haven't seen before, and it's not really unusual based on their long-term volatility
claims.claim: AlphaQuest closed despite a drawdown within its historical range, showing the business decision to return money rather than a statistical failure.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: often managers in the short-term space are more volatility expansion type strategies
claims.claim: Short-term CTAs are often vol-expansion strategies and had a poor environment while equities trended higher, though several did well over the last 12 months.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: they attract kind of capital into those high sharp strategies which tend to reinforce them and that can keep going for a while but at some stage it may blow up
claims.claim: Pod shops attract capital into high-Sharpe strategies, reinforcing them until they eventually blow up.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: classic trend following with fixed-size positions based on the volatility at the entry point wouldn't necessarily do great because the vol is simply too high
claims.claim: Jerry Parker's point: with Bitcoin's huge vol a fixed-size trend system cannot build a meaningful position, and a dynamic position size firm could add as vol falls.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: it still seems to me that in the long run maybe it doesn't make a huge difference
claims.claim: Niels thinks fixed vs dynamic sizing matters little in the long run, but changes how strategies perform from time to time.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: in many years trend has underperformed 60/40, but in a few years it has outperformed, and in those years where it's outperformed, it's massively outperformed
claims.claim: Trend underperforms 60/40 in many years but outperforms massively in a few (2008 and 2022 had about a 40-point differential), which is its diversifying value.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: So, it comes one from what I would call dynamic positioning
claims.claim: Source 1 of differentiation: trend dynamically sizes bond/equity exposure (short bonds and less equity in 2022) instead of holding a static 60/40.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: you might get a you know, a brief dip down in equities, and trend followers will reduce that equity risk
claims.claim: After a brief equity dip trend followers cut risk, and if equities bounce back a static 60% allocation outperforms (whipsaw cost).

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: the second area where you get diversifying qualities from trend following is exposure to commodity markets and currency markets as well
claims.claim: Source 2: long and short positions in commodities and currencies, which captured the 2007 oil run-up, the 2008 sell-off and 2014-15 volatility.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: 2008, it was obviously commodities was a huge driver of performance there
claims.claim: Attribution differs by crisis: commodities led in 2008, while 2022 was mainly dynamic bond/equity adjustment plus long dollar.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: those periods when when 60/40 really suffers are some of the very best periods for trend
claims.claim: Trend has low correlation to 60/40 and does best when 60/40 suffers, the rationale for holding all three.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: it was very clear that the main source of returns during crisis came from the commodity part of the portfolio
claims.claim: A large CTA's sector attribution study showed crisis returns came mainly from commodities.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: more often than not, equities will be a losing proposition or losing position uh for trend followers in the initial phase
claims.claim: In equity crises trend followers usually lose on equities initially, possibly for long, and make money elsewhere.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: that they can actually also deliver positive returns during periods of very strong equity performance, which is something a lot of the other risk mitigation strategies don't do
claims.claim: Trend can deliver in strong equity markets as well as in crises, unlike other risk mitigation strategies.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: because it actually measures the percentage of markets within that 44 market portfolio that it tracks that are quote and quote trending
claims.claim: Niels's trend barometer finished at 55, the share of 44 markets that are trending, indicating a broad, strong trend environment in Feb 2026.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: the equity sector in itself is not necessarily a great sector for trend following
claims.claim: In Niels's data equities are not a strong sector for trend following, while bonds (the 40 of 60/40) have been good.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: we have seen some dispersion linked to that in in kind of metals prices obviously
claims.claim: Dispersion between CTAs was driven by position sizing in metals; more static sizing helped on the upside, with opportunities broadening across equities, metals and bonds.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: not necessarily the strategies that have done best over the last 3 5 years
claims.claim: New hedge fund allocators should pick strategies with a record in major equity downturns (trend, macro, commodities, vol), not recent best performers in a bull market.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: any strategy coupled with the S&P tends to look pretty good
claims.claim: Return stacking and portable alpha packaging make strategies look good only because equities are doing well.

correction.issue: Overstated causality. Alan says packaging track records with other indices is 'totally fair' and merely 'symptomatic' of an equity bull market, where any strategy coupled with the S&P looks good; he does not say the strategies look good only because of the packaging.
correction.fix: Return stacking and portable-alpha presentations are fair but symptomatic of a strong equity environment, where any strategy coupled with the S&P tends to look good, so the packaged track record flatters standalone merit.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: drawing the the inference that it should lead to greater allocations to the pure diversifiers
claims.claim: Total portfolio approach (TPA) may lead to larger allocations to pure diversifiers like trend.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: So, last week was much more about deflation and disinflation and AI and now we're into geopolitics, but you know, things change quickly.
claims.claim: Macro themes flip within a week (AI disinflation to geopolitics), so sentiment toward CTAs and hedge funds can also shift quickly.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: equities start to wobble and at same time CTAs are doing well and people can see trends developing, you know, it doesn't take much for for sentiment to to shift pretty quickly
claims.claim: Allocator sentiment toward CTAs can turn quickly if equities wobble while trend works.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: we actually equalized a record set back in 1999 with eight consecutive positive months
claims.claim: Niels's firm equaled a 1999 record of eight consecutive positive months in February 2026.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: one of the strongest periods of performance and one of the most consistent periods of performance in history
claims.claim: After negative headlines in summer 2025 about tariffs and erratic policy, trend (SG Trend) posted one of its strongest and most consistent runs, a lesson not to rule the strategy out on narrative.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: I think it will be, uh, a boost for our industry because there are so few strategies where you can truly see the, um, the benefit to the total portfolio
claims.claim: Sovereign wealth funds using TPA see trend's portfolio benefit clearly, which should boost allocations.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: what have you got in your portfolio if if you're wrong
claims.claim: Dave Dredge's question: investors adapting portfolios should ask what pays off if their view is wrong.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: I have a feeling that many trend followers flipped their energy position from flat
claims.claim: Many trend followers moved energy from flat/short to long in February, so they were on the right side of the early March oil spike (natural gas small due to vol).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: The initial move or the initial performance is pretty random because we just don't know how we're positioned going into a conflict like this.
claims.claim: Trend followers' performance in the first days of a sudden shock is random since positioning before the event is unknown.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: SocGen CTA index down 1.94%, but still up 6.22% for the year
claims.claim: As of early March 2026: SG CTA -1.94% (YTD +6.22%), SG Trend -1.85% (+6.78%), Short-term traders -0.25% (+3.56%); MSCI World -1.5%, Agg -0.57% in March, so bonds gave no offset.
claims.indicator: SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders indices

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: really heating oil up about 33%
claims.claim: March leaders were heating oil (+33%), crude and gasoline, while losers were silver, platinum, palladium and the Nikkei.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: emphasize that it's not their base case scenario
claims.claim: The Citrini report is an outlier scenario of AI-driven white-collar unemployment and eroded moats, not a forecast.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: like AI is a game changer. It's going to change the economy. It's going to make everything cheaper.
claims.claim: Incoming Fed chair Kevin Warsh (nominated, in May) views AI as a disinflationary productivity boom, supporting rate cuts.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: he held off on raising rates and there's no need because productivity is going to keep inflation in check
claims.claim: Greenspan in 1996 held off hiking because of productivity gains, the precedent Warsh uses for cutting rates.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: But by the end of the decade Greenspan was actually raising rates in '99 and 2000 because the economy was overheating
claims.claim: Per Furman, the 1990s productivity boom was disinflationary at first but ended with rate hikes in 1999-2000 as demand overheated.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: The reason is yes, you have an initial supply shift, but then you also get a demand reaction
claims.claim: A productivity supply shock is followed by a demand response (capex, optimism, wages, wealth effect).

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: the gains would go to the the holder the holders of capital
claims.claim: Productivity gains may go to capital owners rather than wages (Gilded Age: benign deflation, real wage gains lagged).

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: we don't know how big a of an impact it's going to be
claims.claim: Three unknowns for AI: size of impact, who benefits, and demand response.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: the stock market reaction has been has started to get negative as as investors have seen more and more capex
claims.claim: Hyperscaler capex is now met with negative stock reactions, so the capex-boom demand response may already be priced or seen as excessive.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: by its own mandate, the Fed has to counter that to try and pump up inflation via more stimulus
claims.claim: If AI is disinflationary, an inflation-targeting Fed would stimulate during an equity bubble, risking policy error and asset bubbles, with political pressure for cuts.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: may displace white work white collar workers in software, but can they go and retrain as health care workers
claims.claim: AI can ease aggregate supply constraints but leaves labor-market mismatches (white-collar to health care), so imbalances persist.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: the risk of some policy error there has been reasonably strong
claims.claim: Alan sees reasonably strong risk of a Fed policy error later this year and into next, not this month.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: Powell was threatened with going to jail for raising rates or not cutting rates
claims.claim: Political threats to Powell mean a new Fed chair will have easing pressure in mind, though the FOMC is a committee.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: You know, it's it's it's about the perils of following narrative.
claims.claim: Narrative (tariff on/off makes trend following hard) was wrong in 2025; the administration became a driver of trends like gold and the debasement trade.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: usually when these things kind of gets near to their worst ever drawdown, it's really not a bad time to to to invest
claims.claim: Niels argues investing near a trend fund's worst drawdown is attractive, but Alan notes CTAs make the same case at highs and that investors struggle to hold.
claims.testable: yes: test entry vs drawdown depth

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: ignore that narrative and look at the at the statistics
claims.claim: Ignore the prevailing narrative about trend and look at statistics when allocating.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: it's diversification not insurance
claims.claim: 2025 reconfirmed trend is diversification, not insurance: it can lose in the short run.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: You can't evaluate a decision based on one outcome.
claims.claim: Resulting: April 2025 adaptation to equity sell-off cost money when Trump reversed, but the decision was still sound.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: not second-guess how long these moves can go on and not try and time the top
claims.claim: Trend followers' ability to stay with a trend (gold from 4,000 to above 5,000) without timing the top was the 2H 2025 benefit.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: less of a pure defender, more of a midfielder in the sense that trend can go on the attack in terms of be a positive contributor to returns in the pro-risk environments
claims.claim: Trend is a midfielder: contributes in pro-risk periods and tilts the portfolio defensive in stress, a more intuitive description than crisis offset.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: you get a tracking error of about 5% per annum versus the Saxon trend index if you randomly selected two managers
claims.claim: Winton paper: two randomly chosen trend managers give about 5% annual tracking error versus SG Trend index (up to about plus or minus 3% performance gap).

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: if you adjust for that you can get closer to to the index
claims.claim: Matching volatility levels or picking the most correlated managers reduces tracking error; an equal-weight index gives high-vol managers more risk, so alternatively blend less-correlated managers at slightly higher vol.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: the main differentiators for for CTAs in the trend and managed futures space are kind of speed, universe of markets traded, whether you have diversifying non-trend signals or not, and risk management
claims.claim: Winton paper: CTAs differ by speed, market universe, non-trend signals and risk management, so blending managers averages speed and one manager may choose optimal speed better.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: But they do show how managers come and go a lot more in that space than in the trend space.
claims.claim: The SG non-trend CTA index performed well in aggregate, but non-trend managers churn far more than trend managers; benefits of one manager with non-trend signals are fee netting and capital efficiency.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: you do get the additional benefit of the different perspective on portfolio construction
claims.claim: Allocating to separate specialist managers brings different IP and perspective at the cost of fee netting; solutions businesses growth vs niche houses.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: you might actually lose the very thing that you want from your CTA, uh which is convexity
claims.claim: Replicating or blending to smooth an index can remove the convexity that makes CTAs valuable.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: that smoothest ride might not be exactly what you want um in the long run
claims.claim: One or two long-tenured trend followers may beat chasing the smoothest ride.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: the cost of maintaining multiple relationships
claims.claim: Alan has shifted toward fewer managers because understanding a program makes it easier to stick with it, though tension remains with diversification.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: is there a CTA beta
claims.claim: Whether a stable CTA beta exists to benchmark is doubtful; they dismiss the ChatGPT question.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: we did see more of a reaction in European equities as well
claims.claim: European equities reacted more than US ones to the Iran shock, arguably because European gas prices responded even more, so the energy channel (gas) explains regional equity differences.
claims.indicator: European equities vs European gas prices (March 2026)
claims.direction: European equities down more than US
claims.conditions: Specific to the energy shock; US indices were also pinned by option flows.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: there is a lot more differentiation idiosyncratic models, different approaches that managers pursue
claims.claim: Short-term CTAs differ far more in models and approaches than long-term trend managers, so the weakness of the short-term index does not describe every manager and several did well over 12 months.
claims.conditions: Manager selection matters more in the short-term space.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: hard to disentangle the two effects, but there are two distinct effects that I would point to
claims.claim: Splitting trend's edge over 60/40 into dynamic bond/equity positioning versus commodity/currency trading needs year-by-year P&L attribution against a static 60/40; the two effects are hard to disentangle.
claims.conditions: Differs by crisis (2008 commodity-led, 2022 bond/equity-led plus dollar).

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: other strategies that I think are in vogue, global macro for sure
claims.claim: At the March 2026 Miami conference global macro was the strategy in vogue, attracting the most allocator attention alongside portable alpha and return stacking, a sentiment marker for where allocators are crowding.
claims.conditions: Sentiment snapshot; Alan warns that recent bull-market performance is not evidence of downturn behavior.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: less so in terms of alpha generation, but but more and more novel ways of using it
claims.claim: At the conference managers said they use AI in their business processes, but its impact so far is not in alpha generation; the uses are novel workflows even at macro managers.
claims.indicator: AI use by hedge fund managers
claims.conditions: Early stage; no clear takeaway yet.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: it'll be interesting to see how Societe Generale will handle that in the index because they are part of the SocGen CTA index
claims.claim: Manager closures raise an index-construction question: AlphaQuest is in the SG CTA Index and it is unclear how a manager dropping out mid-year is treated, which matters for survivorship bias in CTA benchmarks.
claims.testable: yes - check index rules and history

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: a year ago we were debating was it going to be 0.1% of productivity growth or 0.5
claims.claim: Expectations for AI's productivity effect moved in a year from a debate over 0.1% versus 0.5% to a much bigger expected impact, yet there is no consensus on the policy response, which is where the macro risk sits.
claims.conditions: Policy response (labor-market mismatches versus stimulus) is the open question.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: the prediction market so to speak actually had favored someone else uh, leading up to this
claims.claim: Prediction markets had favored another candidate for Fed chair before Warsh was suddenly named (Alan adds that the Powell proceedings made Hassett's confirmation unlikely), an example of a consensus forecast missing a political outcome.
claims.indicator: prediction market odds for Fed chair
claims.conditions: Political appointments depend on behind-the-scenes deals.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: the middle of 2024 people saying buy the dip in CTAs
claims.claim: Calls to buy CTAs after the mid-2024 dip were early: the drawdown ran about 24 months, so drawdown-based timing can be too early, though some managers have clients who time it successfully; CTAs' first job is keeping investors in.
claims.indicator: CTA drawdown duration and re-entry timing
claims.conditions: A drawdown near the largest ever for the index is a stronger entry signal than a mere dip.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: you going to have tracking error unless you go out and buy all 10 managers
claims.claim: Even replication strategies cannot track a CTA index tightly; tracking error stays material unless one holds all (about ten) index managers, so investors must accept it.
claims.conditions: Smaller with volatility matching or more correlated managers.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, allocator)
claims.quote: whether it makes sense to allocate to trend in traditional as well as alternative
claims.claim: Adding alternative markets expands trend's opportunity set, but the Winton paper raises whether to hold one portfolio or two distinct ones; it is a value call on whether alternative-market access needs a specialist manager.
claims.indicator: traditional vs alternative market trend sleeves
claims.conditions: Depends on operational infrastructure and capability.
claims.testable: partly - compare combined vs separate sleeves
